VBO:0200007.summary: The Africanis is a southern African landrace shaped through long life alongside rural communities. Its lean, muscular frame, wedge-like head and short coat recur across a visibly varied population, with local forms reflecting the places where the dogs live.

sources.title: AfriCanis Society: What is in the name AfriCanis?
sources.evidence: The Africanis Society describes a heterogeneous southern African landrace with a slender muscular frame, conical head and short coat, and explicitly seeks to conserve its variation.

VBO:0200007.interestingFact: AfriCanis joins “Africa” and “Canis,” a name chosen for the indigenous dogs of southern Africa.

VBO:0200009.summary: The Akbash is a white livestock guardian from the plains and mountains of western Turkey. It combines a tall, powerful frame with the reach and agility needed to patrol open grazing country; its pale coat is one of the type’s most consistent features.

sources.title: UKC Akbash Dog standard
sources.evidence: The UKC standard identifies western Turkey, white coat, livestock-guardian work, substantial size, and an athletic frame suited to confronting or pursuing predators.

VBO:0200017.summary: The Alaskan Malamute is a substantial Arctic sled dog made for hauling with strength and endurance. A deep chest, heavy bone, broad head, dense double coat and plume-like tail give it a powerful outline, while varied face markings make individual dogs surprisingly easy to tell apart.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 243: Alaskan Malamute
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives US origin, sled-dog use, substantial body, deep chest, dense double coat, plume tail, face markings, and emphasis on strength and endurance rather than racing speed.

VBO:0200017.interestingFact: Malamutes were shaped for hauling strength and endurance across Arctic ground, with speed a lesser priority.

VBO:0200045.summary: The American English Coonhound is an American scent hound built to follow raccoon trails through long nights in the woods. Long legs, a deep chest and a close coat support ground-covering work; redtick is one familiar pattern, though the breed comes in other accepted colors too.

sources.title: AKC American English Coonhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard identifies raccoon tracking and treeing, endurance, long-legged hound conformation, deep chest, and accepted ticked and other color patterns.

VBO:0200049.summary: The American Hairless Terrier grew from the ratting-terrier tradition but took a striking turn: the hairless variety has exposed skin where a working coat would usually be. It remains small, smoothly muscled and quick on its feet; a coated variety belongs to the same breed.
VBO:0200049.historicalRoots: American Rat Terrier-derived companion and sport terrier.

sources.title: AKC American Hairless Terrier standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard describes a small-to-medium active terrier, ratting ancestry, hairless and coated varieties, and the hairless variety being unsuited to most hunting work.

VBO:0200049.interestingFact: Coated and hairless puppies are both legitimate expressions of the American Hairless Terrier.

VBO:0200062.summary: The Anatolian Shepherd Dog is a large flock guardian from Turkey’s Anatolian plateau. Its substantial but mobile build, thick undercoat and steady watchfulness belong to a dog developed to protect livestock across demanding country.

sources.title: AKC Anatolian Shepherd Dog standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard identifies Anatolian origin, livestock-guarding purpose, large powerful but agile build and thick undercoat.

VBO:0200090.summary: The Australian Kelpie arose for sheep work across the vast, hot and dusty runs of New South Wales and Victoria. Medium-sized and lithe rather than heavy, it was selected to cover difficult ground efficiently; its ancestry includes collie-type dogs brought from Scotland.
VBO:0200090.historicalRoots: Australian sheepdog developed from Scottish collie-type imports.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 293: Australian Kelpie
sources.evidence: FCI standard details vast sheep properties, heat and rough terrain, Scottish collie-type ancestry, and medium agile sheepdog form.

VBO:0200090.interestingFact: On enormous Australian sheep runs, one Kelpie could do the work of several people.

VBO:0200098.summary: The Australian Terrier is a little rough-coated worker developed far from the British terriers that helped shape it. Early Tasmanian and mainland dogs combined practical vermin-catching ability with companionship; the harsh coat and upright, alert outline still show that hard-use origin.
VBO:0200098.historicalRoots: Australian working terrier shaped from British imports.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 8: Australian Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces development in Tasmania, New South Wales and Victoria from British broken-coated terriers and describes its rough-terrain working purpose.

VBO:0200098.interestingFact: It was among the earliest dog breeds developed in Australia, despite drawing on several British terrier lines.

VBO:0200110.summary: The Bakharwal dog belongs to the hill country of Jammu and Kashmir, where Bakarwal and Gujjar communities have kept it with moving flocks. Medium-sized dogs, often with dark coats, accompany livestock into high pastures and watch against predators.
VBO:0200110.historicalRoots: Jammu and Kashmir pastoral livestock guardian.

sources.title: Indian Journal of Tropical Biodiversity: Bakerwal dog survey
sources.evidence: Survey of 36 adult Bakerwal dogs in Poonch measured an average height near 56 cm, found black coats predominant, and describes Bakarwal/Gujjar livestock protection on highland migrations.

VBO:0200110.interestingFact: Its name comes from the Bakarwal pastoral community, whose migrations have long included these dogs.

VBO:0200124.summary: The Basset Bleu de Gascogne brings a big hound's voice and nose to a low, sturdy frame. In France it has hunted rabbit and hare alone or in packs; the mottled black-and-white coat gives the blue impression behind its name, while long ears complete the classic Gascon look.
VBO:0200124.historicalRoots: French rabbit-and-hare scent hound revived in the late nineteenth century.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 35: Basset Bleu de Gascogne
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives French origin, rabbit and hare use, pack work, strong nose, sonorous voice, low basset build, and black-white ticking.

VBO:0200124.interestingFact: The breed was revived by hunters in the late 1800s after its numbers had waned.

VBO:0200131.summary: The Beagle is a compact British scent hound made for following hare at a pace hunters could manage on foot. Its sturdy body, long ears and lifted tail belong to a pack worker whose attention stays on the trail; the familiar sociable face has a very practical hunting history.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 161: Beagle
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Great Britain, hare hunting on foot, pack use, compact sturdy build, long ears and upright tail.

VBO:0200131.interestingFact: The FCI history records that Tudor-era beagles included tiny 'pocket' dogs as well as wirehaired ones.

VBO:0200137.summary: The Bedlington Terrier is a North English terrier with an almost lamb-like outline: a soft topknot, arched body and narrow, pear-shaped head. That delicate-looking silhouette hides a sporting past around the mining districts, where earlier Rothbury terriers hunted rabbits.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 9: Bedlington Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Rothbury mining areas and rabbit hunting, and describes the graceful arched body, pear-shaped head and lamb-like appearance.

VBO:0200137.interestingFact: Before the Bedlington name took hold, the breed was known as the Rothbury Terrier.

VBO:0200161.summary: The Bernese Mountain Dog is a long-coated tricolor farm dog from the country around Bern. Its size and strength served guarding, cattle driving and cart work; the broad white blaze, rust points and black coat now make one of the Swiss mountain dogs instantly recognizable.
VBO:0200161.historicalRoots: Bernese farm guard, draught and cattle dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 45: Bernese Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard locates the breed around Bern, describes farm guard, draught and cattle work, and specifies the long tricolor coat.

VBO:0200161.interestingFact: It was once called the Dürrbächler after a hamlet and inn near Riggisberg where these dogs were common.

VBO:0200174.summary: The Black Russian Terrier is a large, robust Russian working dog whose dense black coat forms a beard and brows around a strong head. Developed for guard and service work in the twentieth century, it carries more substance than the terrier name suggests, with a broad chest and slightly rectangular frame.
VBO:0200174.historicalRoots: Twentieth-century Russian guard and service dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 327: Black Russian Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes deliberate Russian development for service and guard work, large robust build, black rough coat, beard and eyebrows.

VBO:0200174.interestingFact: Despite its name, the Black Russian Terrier sits among working molossoid and pinscher-type breeds in FCI classification.

VBO:0200189.summary: The Bolognese is a little white Italian companion with a compact, nearly square body and a long coat that stands away in soft flocks. It passed through European courtly life as a prized gift and appears in paintings by several celebrated artists.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 196: Bolognese
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies Italy, companion use, compact square build, white flocked coat, court gifts and appearances in European paintings.

VBO:0200189.interestingFact: The FCI history notes Bolognese in works by Titian, Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Goya.

VBO:0200197.summary: The Borzoi is a tall Russian sighthound built for fast pursuit across open ground. Its long narrow head, deep chest and flowing coat give it elegance at rest, but the historical task was demanding: chasing hare and fox, with wolf hunting a smaller part of the tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 193: Borzoi
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Russian origin, hare and fox pursuit with less common wolf hunting, great speed and endurance, and long-coated sighthound form.

VBO:0200197.interestingFact: The formal Russian name Russkaya Psovaya Borzaya points to its long-coated hunting-hound identity.

VBO:0200210.summary: The Boxer is a compact, muscular German dog with a square frame, smooth coat and unmistakable broad muzzle. Its immediate ancestor, the Brabant Bullenbeisser, was used by hunters to hold game until people arrived; selective breeding carried that powerful jaw into a modern working and companion breed.
VBO:0200210.historicalRoots: German Bullenbeisser-descended hunting and working dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 144: Boxer
sources.evidence: FCI standard names the Brabant Bullenbeisser ancestor, explains game-holding work and selection for a broad muzzle, and describes compact square muscular build.

VBO:0200210.interestingFact: Its short, wide muzzle traces to a specific hunting task: gripping and holding game brought up by hounds.

VBO:0200232.summary: The Brazilian Tracker is a large scent hound shaped from American Foxhound stock for Brazilian hunting country. It was selected for tracking and cornering game, then rebuilt after a severe population decline in the late twentieth century; the modern dog carries a particularly unusual restoration story.
VBO:0200232.historicalRoots: Brazilian foxhound-derived tracking and hunting breed.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 275: Brazilian Tracker
sources.evidence: FCI standard names American Foxhound-based selection by Osvaldo Aranha Filho, Brazilian field use, and breeding resumption after a 1970s–2000 setback.

VBO:0200232.interestingFact: The breed was first recognized in 1967, then its breeding had to be resumed after a major decline.

VBO:0200255.summary: The Bull Terrier is a muscular British terrier whose long, uninterrupted egg-shaped head is unlike any other dog’s. James Hinks established the recognizable type in the 1850s, balancing a distinctive face with a strongly built, agile body.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 11: Bull Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard credits James Hinks in the 1850s, describes the egg-shaped head and muscular body, and states that no fixed size or weight limit is imposed.

VBO:0200255.interestingFact: The first Bull Terrier in its modern form was shown at Birmingham in 1862.

VBO:0200267.summary: The Cairn Terrier is a small Scottish earthdog built for rough ground, with strong quarters, upright ears and a weather-resistant, shaggy coat. Its tidy size should not obscure the point of the build: a hardy, flexible terrier able to work among stone and brush.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 4: Cairn Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives British origin and describes a small agile working terrier with deep rib, strong quarters, erect ears and weather-resistant coat.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: Cairn Terrier
sources.evidence: Places the breed in the Scottish Western Highlands and Isle of Skye, where it worked vermin among rocky cairns.

VBO:0200267.interestingFact: Its deliberately natural coat and workmanlike outline distinguish it from more sculpted terrier silhouettes.

VBO:0200273.summary: The Can de Palleiro is Galicia’s traditional farm dog, named for the hayloft where it often slept. Sturdy and agile, it helped drive and guard livestock across Galician holdings, with a shepherd-like outline shaped by farm work.

sources.title: Xunta de Galicia: Can de Palleiro
sources.evidence: Xunta de Galicia breed page identifies the Galician farm setting, the hayloft origin of the name, shepherding and guarding roles, and substantial shepherd-dog morphology.

VBO:0200273.interestingFact: Palleiro means hayloft or straw barn: the breed's name remembers its place on Galician farms.

VBO:0200299.summary: The Catalan Sheepdog comes from the Catalan Pyrenees, where a medium, shaggy-coated dog kept flocks moving through mountain and pasture country. Its slightly long body and abundant rough coat give it a soft outline, but the history behind that coat is practical sheep work.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 87: Catalan Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names the Catalan Pyrenees and flock-driving use, and describes medium size, slightly long proportions and abundant coat.

VBO:0200299.interestingFact: Its Catalan name, Gos d'Atura Català, keeps the regional identity front and center.

VBO:0200321.summary: The Central Asian Shepherd Dog is a massive guardian shaped across a huge region between the Caspian, the southern Urals, China and Afghanistan. Protection of herds, caravans and homes favored a strong, economical build suited to harsh conditions, with considerable regional variation still visible.
VBO:0200321.historicalRoots: Central Asian herd, caravan and homestead guardian.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 335: Central Asian Shepherd Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives broad Central Asian geographic range, herds/caravans/dwellings protection, harsh natural selection and powerful mountain-type form.

VBO:0200321.interestingFact: The breed's historical range spans many present-day borders, so one modern country cannot tell its whole story.

VBO:0200344.summary: The Chinese Chongqing Dog is a compact, muscular dog from southwestern China with a remarkably spare coat and upright, bamboo-like tail. Its broad head, strong cheeks and nearly square body make a bold silhouette at medium size.
VBO:0200344.historicalRoots: Southwestern Chinese hunting and guarding tradition.

sources.title: Chongqing Pet Association breed standard
sources.evidence: Chongqing Pet Association standard specifies medium nearly square muscular form, short sparse coat, broad head and distinctive upright tail.

VBO:0200344.interestingFact: Bluish-black patches on the tongue are a characteristic of the Chinese Chongqing Dog.

VBO:0200354.summary: The Chippiparai is a lean Tamil Nadu sighthound whose light frame, broad chest and tucked abdomen suit fast pursuit. This medium-sized regional dog is especially associated with the Tirunelveli breeding tract of southern Tamil Nadu.

sources.title: Indian Journal of Veterinary Sciences: Chippiparai study
sources.evidence: Veterinary field study identifies a medium indigenous sighthound in southern Tamil Nadu, especially Tirunelveli, with fawn coat, broad chest and tucked abdomen.

VBO:0200354.interestingFact: Fawn coat, dark nostrils and dark eyes are characteristic of the Chippiparai dogs documented in southern Tamil Nadu.

VBO:0200365.summary: The Cirneco dell'Etna is a fine-coated Sicilian rabbit hunter with a nearly square body and large upright ears. Its compact, slender frame belongs to rocky country around Mount Etna, where speed and agile footing mattered more than bulk.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 199: Cirneco dell'Etna
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Sicily and rabbit hunting, ancient regional presence, square lean conformation, fine coat and erect ears.

VBO:0200365.interestingFact: Ancient Sicilian coins and mosaics show dogs of the Cirneco type centuries before modern breed records.

VBO:0200397.summary: The Curly Coated Retriever is a tall British gundog whose body is covered in small, tight curls while the face stays smooth. The unusual coat gives a crisp, sculptural outline, but it belongs to a capable retrieving dog with strong limbs and a little more height than many people expect.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 110: Curly Coated Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard states British origin and retrieving use, upstanding strong form, slightly long proportions, tight crisp curls and smooth face.

VBO:0200429.summary: The Dandie Dinmont Terrier is a low, long British terrier with a curved body, short strong legs and a silky crown of hair. Large dark eyes soften the look, while a weatherproof coat and working-terrier build recall its practical country roots.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 168: Dandie Dinmont Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes the low long body, short strong legs, silky head covering, large eyes and weatherproof coat.

VBO:0200429.interestingFact: Its coat colors have wonderfully specific names: pepper and mustard.

VBO:0200445.summary: The Dogo Argentino is a powerful white hunting dog developed in Córdoba for large game. Dr. Antonio Nores Martínez combined several lines around the old Córdoba fighting dog, then selected for stamina and a strong but athletic body suited to Argentine countryside.
VBO:0200445.historicalRoots: Córdoba big-game hunting dog developed in the twentieth century.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 292: Dogo Argentino
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Córdoba, Antonio Nores Martínez, the old Córdoba dog and big-game purpose, and specifies a powerful white athletic form.

VBO:0200445.interestingFact: The breed's all-white coat was an intentional part of its founder's selection.

VBO:0200453.summary: The Drentsche Patrijshond is a Dutch partridge dog rooted in Drenthe, where older spaniel-type hunting dogs remained comparatively distinct. It can point, search and retrieve, carrying its work in a sturdy, feathered brown-and-white frame with a notably full tail.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 224: Drentsche Patrijshond
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces the breed to Drenthe and sixteenth-century partridge dogs, gives pointing work, and describes a brown-white feathered coat and full tail.

VBO:0200453.interestingFact: Its name literally ties the dog to Drenthe and to patrijs, the Dutch word for partridge.

VBO:0200463.summary: The Dutch Shepherd grew around the edges of Dutch fields as much as among the sheep. It patrolled crop boundaries, moved flocks to market and helped with farm chores; its athletic, brindled body comes in short, long and rough-coated varieties.
VBO:0200463.historicalRoots: Dutch sheep and farm-boundary working dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 223: Dutch Shepherd
sources.evidence: FCI standard details field-boundary patrol, sheep and farm duties, brindled coat, and short-, long- and rough-haired varieties.

VBO:0200463.interestingFact: Keeping sheep out of planted fields was one of its signature jobs, a kind of moving fence before modern barriers.

VBO:0200495.summary: The English Setter is an elegant British pointing dog with long feathering and a light, ground-covering stride. Its flecked 'belton' coat can look almost painted, yet the fine outline has a field purpose: locating game birds and holding a point for the hunter.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 2: English Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies British pointing use, elegant medium frame, feathering, distinctive belton flecking and active game sense.

VBO:0200495.interestingFact: Belton is the traditional name for the breed's fine ticking, seen in several color combinations.

VBO:0200508.summary: The Estonian Hound is a medium scent hound developed for hare, fox and lynx. A 1950s effort to favor a lower hound shaped its size; the clean white markings and firm, athletic frame make it visible and useful through northern hunting country.
VBO:0200508.historicalRoots: Estonian hare, fox and lynx hound standardized in 1954.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 366: Estonian Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard names hare/fox/lynx use, intentional lower height, 1954 approval, medium firm build and visible white markings.

VBO:0200508.interestingFact: Thousands of hounds were evaluated before Estonia approved the breed in 1954.

VBO:0200519.summary: The Field Spaniel is a low, substantial British flushing dog with a long, glossy coat and an unhurried country-dog look. It was shaped from older spaniel lines for finding and retrieving game; after two sharp population declines, dedicated breeders kept this quieter branch of the spaniel family alive.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 123: Field Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes flushing/retrieving work, Sussex Springer and Cocker contributions, long coat and two historical near-losses.

VBO:0200519.interestingFact: The breed came close to disappearing twice: once through early-twentieth-century fashion and again later in the century.

VBO:0200528.summary: The Flat-Coated Retriever is a British gundog with a long, clean head, athletic frame and smooth feathered coat in black or liver. Built to carry game without heaviness, it keeps a distinctive streamlined outline among retrievers, especially in the level line from head through muzzle.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 121: Flat-Coated Retriever
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives British gundog use, medium athletic build, long head with slight stop, feathered flat coat and black or liver color.

VBO:0200528.interestingFact: A very slight stop gives the long head an almost uninterrupted line from skull to muzzle.

VBO:0200550.summary: The French Water Dog, or Barbet, is a woolly-coated French waterfowl hunter whose beard gives it its name. It searches and flushes birds from aquatic vegetation before retrieving them, so the dense curls and substantial coat belong to wet, cold work rather than decoration.
VBO:0200550.historicalRoots: French waterfowl flushing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 105: French Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names sixteenth-century French waterfowl history, searching/flushing/retrieving in water vegetation, thick woolly coat and beard etymology.

VBO:0200550.interestingFact: Barbet comes from barbe, French for beard, the feature that frames its face.

VBO:0201454.summary: The German Pinscher is a medium, square-built German watchdog with a short, close coat and clean, athletic lines. It shares early ancestry with the Schnauzer; what separated the smooth-haired Pinscher was its coat, making a strikingly different silhouette from a related working stock.
VBO:0201454.historicalRoots: German smooth-coated watch and companion dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 184: German Pinscher
sources.evidence: FCI standard cites nineteenth-century German records, shared ancestry with the rough-coated Schnauzer, smooth short coat and square medium build.

VBO:0201454.interestingFact: Older records called the Schnauzer the rough-coated Pinscher, reflecting their shared roots.

VBO:0200602.summary: The German Wirehaired Pointer was deliberately shaped as a versatile gundog for field, forest and water. Its harsh weatherproof coat, beard and brows give a rugged face, while the balanced athletic body answers a demanding brief: search, point and retrieve before and after the shot.
VBO:0200602.historicalRoots: German all-terrain pointing and retrieving gundog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 98: German Wirehaired Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI standard documents late-nineteenth-century development, field/wood/water use, versatile gundog purpose and harsh wire coat with furnishings.

VBO:0200602.interestingFact: Its German name, Deutsch Drahthaar, directly names the wire coat that protects it at work.

VBO:0200613.summary: The Gordon Setter is a substantial Scottish pointing dog, black with sharply placed tan markings and long feathering. Developed around Gordon Castle, it carries more weight and a deeper color scheme than other setters, yet retains the sweeping lines of a bird dog meant to cover open ground.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: Gordon Setter
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes pointing use, substantial galloping build and black-and-tan feathered coat; Royal Kennel Club breed history connects development to Gordon Castle.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 6: Gordon Setter
sources.evidence: Specifies pointing use, substantial galloping build and black-and-tan feathered coat.

VBO:0200613.interestingFact: The name comes from the Dukes of Gordon, whose kennels helped shape the breed.

VBO:0200631.summary: The Greater Swiss Mountain Dog is the short-coated heavyweight of the Swiss mountain-dog family. Farmers used its strong, tricolor body for watching property, pulling loads and moving cattle; despite the size, the outline remains practical and mobile rather than lumbering.
VBO:0200631.historicalRoots: Swiss watch, draught and droving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 58: Greater Swiss Mountain Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Swiss origin, watch/draught/droving roles, large tricolor build and short double coat.

VBO:0200631.interestingFact: At a 1908 Swiss show, two short-haired dogs helped Albert Heim recognize this old large mountain-dog type as distinct.

VBO:0200655.summary: The Hamiltonstövare is a Swedish scent hound bred to pursue hare and fox while giving voice on the trail. It hunts individually rather than as a pack, and its clean tricolor coat, medium athletic frame and long ears place it firmly in the Scandinavian hound tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 132: Hamiltonstovare
sources.evidence: FCI standard specifies hare and fox hunting with voice, non-pack work, Sweden origin, and medium tricolor hound conformation.

VBO:0200655.interestingFact: The breed carries the name of Count Adolf Patrik Hamilton, an important figure in Swedish dog breeding.

VBO:0200671.summary: The Hokkaido is a sturdy Japanese hunting spitz associated with the island's Ainu people and its snowy climate. A harsh double coat, pricked ears and curled or sickle tail frame a compact, strong dog historically used on bear and other game.
VBO:0200671.historicalRoots: Hokkaido hunting dog associated with Ainu communities.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 261: Hokkaido
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Ainu bear hunting, cold/snow adaptation, medium sturdy build, harsh double coat, erect ears and curled or sickle tail.

VBO:0200671.interestingFact: It was designated a Japanese natural monument in 1937, when the regional name Hokkaido became official.

VBO:0200683.summary: The Huntaway is a New Zealand farm dog selected for its voice as much as its legs. Broadly built and variable in coat, it uses a deep bark to push sheep through yards and across steep pasture, announcing its position across the hills.
VBO:0200683.historicalRoots: New Zealand voiced sheep-driving working dog.

sources.title: Te Ara: Farm dogs
sources.evidence: Te Ara describes huntaways as strong farm dogs selected for deep barking, sheep work in yards and open terrain, and variable size and coat.

VBO:0200683.interestingFact: On a working farm, a huntaway's bark is an instruction to stock and a way for the handler to follow the dog's position.

VBO:0200695.summary: The Indian Pariah Dog, often called INDog, is an indigenous village-dog landrace of the Indian subcontinent. A moderate frame, upright ears, short coat and curved tail recur across rural populations whose local histories and colors vary.

sources.title: INDog Project: indigenous village dog
sources.evidence: INDog Project identifies an indigenous free-ranging village-dog type distinct from generic mixed-breed dogs and documents recurring morphology and local landrace variation.

VBO:0200695.interestingFact: The INDog Project distinguishes the indigenous type from the much broader category of all street dogs.

VBO:0200705.summary: The Irish Water Spaniel is a tall, tightly curled waterfowl dog with a smooth face and a startlingly bare-looking 'rat tail.' It has long worked in marsh and heavy cover, hunting and retrieving for wildfowlers; the dense liver curls protect the body while the tail keeps its own distinctive shape.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 124: Irish Water Spaniel
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Irish origin, wildfowling use, dense liver curls, smooth face and distinctive rat tail.

VBO:0200705.interestingFact: Its nearly naked tapering tail is so unusual that it has long been used as a clue in discussions of the breed's ancestry.

VBO:0200710.summary: The Istrian Wire-Haired Hound is a Croatian scent hound whose coarse white coat and orange markings suit the cold, stony hills of the eastern Adriatic. It follows hare, fox and boar with stamina; the beard and rough texture set it apart from its smoother Istrian relative.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 152: Istrian Wire-Haired Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Croatian origin, eastern-Adriatic cold hill habitat, hare/fox/boar hunting, harsh white-orange coat and beard.

VBO:0200710.interestingFact: A 1719 manuscript describes the wire-haired Istrian hound, and says its breeding was already established earlier.

VBO:0200724.summary: The Jack Russell Terrier began with Reverend John Russell's English fox-hunting dogs and was further developed in Australia. The small, flexible body is a little longer than tall, suited to going to ground; smooth, broken and rough coats all belong to the same working-terrier design.
VBO:0200724.historicalRoots: English fox-terrier line developed further in Australia.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 345: Jack Russell Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard names John Russell, English fox-hunting origin, Australian development, earth work, longer-than-tall proportions and three coat types.

VBO:0200724.interestingFact: The taller square Parson Russell and the shorter, longer-bodied Jack Russell took separate paths from related working stock.

VBO:0200735.summary: The Japanese Chin is a tiny, fine-boned companion with a broad face, large dark eyes and a silky coat that falls in a mane-like ruff. Its upright carriage and plumed tail make a distinctly courtly silhouette; the breed's history belongs to East Asian palace companionship rather than field work.
VBO:0200735.historicalRoots: East Asian court companion developed in Japan.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 206: Japanese Chin
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Japanese patronage, small square fine-boned build, broad face, silky coat, ruff and tail carried over the back.

VBO:0200747.summary: The Kai Ken comes from the mountain-ringed Kai district of Japan, where it was used for deer and boar. A compact, well-muscled body, erect ears and curled tail place it among Japanese spitz types, but the brindle coat gives it a sharply individual identity.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 317: Kai Ken
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Kai district, deer and boar hunting, sturdy medium build, pricked ears, curled tail and brindle coat.

VBO:0200747.interestingFact: Kai tora-ken, an alternate name, evokes the tiger-like striping of the brindle coat.

VBO:0200754.summary: The Karelian Bear Dog is a black-and-white Nordic hunting spitz bred to hold elk or bear at bay with its bark. Sturdy rather than oversized, it has an erect-eared, dense-coated outline suited to northern forests and the stamina to keep large game in place for the hunter.
VBO:0200754.historicalRoots: Karelian and Finnish big-game hunting spitz.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 48: Karelian Bear Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Karelian foundation stock, Finnish development, elk/bear baying work, medium dense-coated spitz form and black-white coloring.

VBO:0200754.interestingFact: The breed was formalized in 1945, with its first dogs registered the following year.

VBO:0200764.summary: The Kerry Blue Terrier is an Irish farm and sporting terrier whose soft, wavy coat matures into shades of slate blue. It once tackled vermin, badger and even otter; the clipped show outline is only one expression of a robust, long-legged working dog.
VBO:0200764.historicalRoots: Irish all-round farm and sporting terrier.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 3: Kerry Blue Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Irish origin, vermin/badger/otter work, long-legged terrier build and soft blue coat.

VBO:0200764.interestingFact: Kerry Blue puppies are born black; the blue coloring develops as the coat matures.

VBO:0200778.summary: The Kombai comes from the Theni district of Tamil Nadu, with a name tied to Kombai village. It is a medium-sized, strong-bodied dog, usually light brown to tan, with a history of guarding farms and households in the region.

sources.title: Veterinary Practitioner: phenotypic characterization of Kombai dogs
sources.evidence: Field survey of 61 adult Kombai dogs in Theni describes Kombai village origin, guarding use, medium adult size and light-brown-to-tan coats.

VBO:0200793.summary: The Kuvasz is a large white Hungarian flock guardian with a strong frame and a dense, gently waved coat. Its roots reach the Carpathian basin, where protecting stock against predators shaped a dog able to watch open country without needing to herd the animals itself.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 54: Kuvasz
sources.evidence: FCI standard describes Magyar-era Carpathian roots, flock protection, large white build and waved dense coat.

VBO:0200793.interestingFact: The breed also appears in Hungarian hunting history during the reign of King Matthias Corvinus.

VBO:0200816.summary: The Large Münsterländer is a black-and-white German pointing dog with feathering and an athletic, balanced frame. Bred as a versatile gundog, it searches field, forest and water and retrieves after the shot; its color history is intertwined with the German longhaired pointing-dog family.
VBO:0200816.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 118: Large Munsterlander
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives German origin, black-white long coat, field/forest/water work, and ties to the longhaired German pointing-dog family.

VBO:0200816.interestingFact: Its distinct breeding line grew after black-and-white dogs were excluded from the German Longhaired Pointer club.

VBO:0200836.summary: The Löwchen is a small French companion whose traditional lion trim turns a long, flowing coat into a dramatic silhouette. The haircut is old rather than a modern novelty: little lion dogs appear in European carving, tapestries and paintings across several centuries.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 233: Lowchen
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives French origin, companion role, traditional lion clip, and depictions in Amiens Cathedral and later tapestries.

VBO:0200836.interestingFact: Stone carvings at Amiens Cathedral show little lion dogs resembling the breed.

VBO:0200865.summary: The Maremma Sheepdog is a large white Italian flock guardian from a tradition linking the Tuscan Maremma with Abruzzo's sheep country. Seasonal movement of flocks helped bring those regional dogs together; the thick pale coat and substantial body remain part of a working landscape.
VBO:0200865.historicalRoots: Italian Abruzzo and Maremma flock-protection dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 201: Maremma Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard traces Abruzzo and Tuscan Maremma guardian strains, seasonal flock migration and crossing, with large robust white-coated form.

VBO:0200865.interestingFact: Transhumance—the seasonal movement of livestock—helped join the Abruzzo and Maremma dogs into the modern breed.

VBO:0200896.summary: The Miniature Schnauzer condenses the German Schnauzer look into a small, sturdy square body. Harsh coat, strong brows and a bristling beard give it a serious expression; the breed arose around Frankfurt from smaller rough-haired pinscher stock at the turn of the twentieth century.
VBO:0200896.historicalRoots: German small rough-haired pinscher and Schnauzer tradition.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 183: Miniature Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI standard places development around Frankfurt, notes rough-haired dwarf Pinscher roots, and describes square strong build, harsh coat, brows and beard.

VBO:0200896.interestingFact: Early breeders worked through varied coat textures to establish the familiar wiry miniature Schnauzer outline.

VBO:0200921.summary: The Mudi is a nimble Hungarian herding dog with pricked ears, a wedge head and a wavy coat over the body. Developed from regional stock in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, it was used on demanding livestock as well as in farmyard watch work.
VBO:0200921.historicalRoots: Hungarian herding dog from local and prick-eared German stock.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 238: Mudi
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Hungarian origin, eighteenth–nineteenth-century development, large-livestock herding, watch work, pricked ears and wavy body coat.

VBO:0200921.interestingFact: Its coat changes texture across the dog: the head and fronts of the legs are short-haired while the body is waved or lightly curled.

VBO:0200935.summary: The New Zealand Heading Dog is an upright, long-legged sheep worker descended from Border Collie stock. It casts around a flock and holds animals with eye and position rather than the Huntaway's voice; a short coat and quick reactions suit close work on large hill farms.
VBO:0200935.historicalRoots: New Zealand sheep-heading dog developed from Border Collies.

sources.title: Te Ara: Farm dogs
sources.evidence: Te Ara describes Border Collie ancestry, upright long-legged smooth coat, casting and close eye work, and the distinction from barking Huntaways.

VBO:0200935.interestingFact: Handlers usually discourage barking in a heading dog, while they deliberately select for a deep bark in Huntaways.

VBO:0200955.summary: The Norwegian Elkhound is a compact gray Nordic hunting dog with a thick weatherproof coat, upright ears and a tightly curled tail. Traditionally it tracked moose through rough terrain, then held the animal's attention with barking and agile movement until the hunter caught up.

sources.title: AKC Norwegian Elkhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard describes gray medium square build, dense coat, erect ears, curled tail, and tracking and baying moose.

VBO:0000668.summary: The Old Danish Pointing Dog is a sturdy brown-and-white Danish bird dog, heavier and calmer in outline than many pointing breeds. Its story is unusually specific: around 1710, Morten Bak of Glenstrup began crossing local farm dogs with traveling dogs, establishing the old Bakhound line.
VBO:0000668.historicalRoots: Danish bird-pointing dog founded near Glenstrup.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 281: Old Danish Pointing Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names bird-gundog role, brown-white piebald form, Morten Bak at Glenstrup around 1710 and early Bakhound breeding.

VBO:0000668.interestingFact: The alternative name Bakhound remembers Morten Bak, the breeder tied to the line's early development.

VBO:0200989.summary: The Patagonian Sheepdog is a Chilean worker from the southern sheep country, shaped by geographic isolation and generations of herding selection. Its medium frame, long or semi-long coat and often partly folded ears suit the rough climate of Aysén and Magallanes.

sources.title: Diversity: Patagonian Sheepdog historical perspective
sources.evidence: Primary historical study documents sheep work and distribution in Chilean Patagonia, geographic isolation, regional genetic continuity and variable working-dog morphology.

VBO:0201016.summary: The Pharaoh Hound is Malta’s fine-lined rabbit hunter, moving with both sight and scent and listening closely when quarry is near. Its lean russet coat, large upright ears and flesh-colored nose make a clear Mediterranean silhouette.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 248: Pharaoh Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Malta origin, sight/scent/ear hunting use, lean athletic form, upright ears, red coat and flesh-colored nose.

VBO:0201035.summary: The Polish Lowland Sheepdog is a compact, muscular herder wrapped in a long, thick coat. A little longer than tall, it historically moved sheep and watched property; the heavy fringe may hide its eyes, but the dog beneath is a sturdy all-weather worker.
VBO:0201035.historicalRoots: Polish lowland herding and farm-watch dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 251: Polish Lowland Sheepdog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Poland, sheepdog and guard roles, compact muscular 9:10 proportions and thick long coat.

VBO:0201035.interestingFact: The breed is often known by the initials PON, from its Polish name Polski Owczarek Nizinny.

VBO:0201064.summary: The Porcelaine is a refined French scent hound with a gleaming white coat, orange patches and finely shaped head. Bred to drive small game toward waiting guns, it combines a light, elegant appearance with the sturdy legs and nose expected of a working pack hound.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 30: Porcelaine
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives French origin, small-game hunting, refined medium hound build, white coat with orange markings and finely sculpted head.

VBO:0201077.summary: The Portuguese Water Dog worked along Portugal's coast, assisting fishing crews and retrieving from the water. Strong shoulders, a muscular body and either wavy or curly coat fit that swimming life; the Algarve became a center for the breed as fishing practices changed elsewhere.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 37: Portuguese Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard records coastwide fishing assistance, later Algarve concentration, swimming musculature and two coat types.

VBO:0201105.summary: The Pumi is a Hungarian herder with a curly coat, narrow muzzle and ears that stand up before tipping forward. It took shape from Puli-type dogs crossed with prick-eared continental terrier types, producing a springy, alert farm worker suited even to larger stock.
VBO:0201105.historicalRoots: Hungarian herder shaped from Puli and continental terrier types.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 56: Pumi
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Hungarian seventeenth–eighteenth-century Puli/terrier-type crossing, herding including large stock, and distinctive tipped ears and curly coat.

VBO:0201105.interestingFact: It was recognized as a separate breed in the early twentieth century after long sharing roots with the Puli.

VBO:0201122.summary: The Rajapalayam is a medium dog from southern Tamil Nadu, with a compact body, white coat and tucked abdomen. Dropped ears, pale pink nose and eyelids, golden eyes and a gently curved tail give it a distinctive look around its namesake town.
VBO:0201122.historicalRoots: Rajapalayam district, Tamil Nadu indigenous working dog.

sources.title: ICAR: phenotypic characterization of Rajapalayam
sources.evidence: ICAR survey of 88 adults in Rajapalayam/Virudhunagar identifies medium compact white dogs with tucked abdomen, pink nose and eyelids, dropped ears, golden eyes, semi-curved tail, and farm-guarding use.

VBO:0201122.interestingFact: The Rajapalayam takes its name from a town in Virudhunagar district, where local dogs have traditionally guarded farms and farmhouses.

VBO:0201137.summary: The Romagna Water Dog began as a curly-coated retriever in the marshes around Ravenna and Comacchio. When those wetlands were drained, its exceptional nose found a new purpose in truffle searching; the compact square body and dense woolly curls still echo its water-dog past.
VBO:0201137.historicalRoots: Romagna marsh retriever turned truffle-searching dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 298: Romagna Water Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Ravenna/Comacchio marsh retrieving, land drainage, truffle-searching shift, near-square build and dense curly coat.

VBO:0201137.interestingFact: Few breeds have such a clear job change: from retrieving in marsh water to finding truffles in the hills.

VBO:0201160.summary: The Saint Bernard is a giant Swiss mountain dog whose name is inseparable from the hospice at the Great St. Bernard Pass. Large dogs there guarded the refuge and later helped find travelers lost in snow and fog; today's breed retains the immense frame, broad head and short- or long-haired coats.
VBO:0201160.historicalRoots: Great St. Bernard Pass hospice and alpine rescue dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 61: Saint Bernard
sources.evidence: FCI standard recounts the hospice, guard and rescue work, giant frame, broad head, and short/long coat varieties.

VBO:0201160.interestingFact: The hospice's dogs appear in records from the 1600s and became renowned for rescue work in the mountain pass.

VBO:0201181.summary: The Schapendoes is a light Dutch sheepdog under a profuse, slightly wavy coat, with a shaggy face and long feathered tail. Heathland shepherds valued its speed, endurance and jumping ability when flocks ranged far from villages; the floating outline hides a nimble worker.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 313: Schapendoes
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives Netherlands heathland sheep-work history, 40–50 cm light build, mobility and jumping, long waved coat and feathered tail.

VBO:0201181.interestingFact: The breed nearly vanished as Dutch sheep flocks declined, then was rebuilt by enthusiasts in the twentieth century.

VBO:0201195.summary: The Scottish Deerhound is a giant rough-coated sighthound shaped to chase red deer across Scottish open country. Its long legs, deep chest and wiry cloak give the impression of a larger, shaggy Greyhound, but the scale reflects a quarry that demanded speed, strength and endurance together.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 164: Scottish Deerhound
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Scottish red-deer hunting over centuries, giant rough-coated Greyhound-like build and speed/power/endurance requirements.

VBO:0201207.summary: The Serbian Hound is a medium Balkan scent hound in warm red tones with a black saddle across the back. Built with strong legs and close coat for long tracking days, it preserves a regional hunting tradition once cataloged under the broader name Balkan Hound.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 150: Serbian Hound
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Serbian origin, former Balkan Hound name, medium robust form, red coat with black mantle, and scent-hound use.

VBO:0201207.interestingFact: The name changed from Balkan Hound to Serbian Hound to reflect where the breed was most established.

VBO:0201225.summary: The Shikoku is a medium Japanese mountain dog developed for wild boar hunting in Kochi Prefecture. Pricked ears, a tightly carried tail and sesame coat mark its spitz silhouette, while the compact, strong body suited steep, difficult terrain.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 319: Shikoku
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Kochi boar hunting, Awa/Hongawa/Hata regional strains, agile mountain build, erect ears and sesame coat.

VBO:0201225.interestingFact: Its older local strains carried the names Awa, Hongawa and Hata, each tied to a breeding area.

VBO:0201240.summary: The Skye Terrier is a long, low Scottish terrier whose straight fall of hair can nearly touch the ground. It came from the Western Isles working-terrier tradition; beneath the dramatic coat is a strong, short-legged dog, and both erect and dropped ears belong to the breed.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 75: Skye Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard places roots in the Western Isles and describes low long body, profuse straight coat, short legs and prick- or drop-ear varieties.

VBO:0201240.interestingFact: Greyfriars Bobby, a Skye Terrier remembered for his vigil by his owner’s Edinburgh grave, has a memorial near the churchyard.

VBO:0201296.summary: The Staffordshire Bull Terrier is a compact, smooth-coated British bull-type terrier with strength well beyond its size. A broad skull, pronounced cheek muscles and sturdy legs frame an agile dog whose short coat leaves its athletic structure in plain view.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 76: Staffordshire Bull Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives British origin and describes smooth coat, broad skull, pronounced cheeks, compact muscular strength and agility.

VBO:0201316.summary: The Swedish Vallhund is a low, long-bodied Swedish farm spitz built to work around cattle. Short strong legs, erect ears and a dense sable coat with pale 'harness' markings make a memorable outline; the tail may take several natural forms.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 14: Swedish Vallhund
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies Swedish origin, heeler use, low sturdy proportions, erect ears, sable coat and harness markings, and natural variation in tail length.

VBO:0201316.interestingFact: The breed was brought back to wider attention after a 1940s search found surviving old-type dogs in West Gotha.

VBO:0201347.summary: The Thai Bangkaew Dog is a square-built spitz from Bangkaew village in Phitsanulok province. A dense stand-off coat, foxlike face and plumed tail give it a crisp outline; local breeding turned a village dog into a breed recognized across Thailand.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 358: Thai Bangkaew Dog
sources.evidence: FCI standard names Bangkaew village and Phitsanulok, describes square spitz build, dense coat, pointed face and plumed tail, and records regional breeding.

VBO:0201347.interestingFact: The FCI history connects the breed's name directly to Bangkaew village, its place of origin.

VBO:0201353.summary: The Tibetan Terrier is a shaggy, medium-sized Tibetan dog whose name is a historical misfit: it is not a true terrier. A sturdy square frame, long coat and broad feet served herding and travel with traders; it later became best known as a companion.
VBO:0201353.historicalRoots: Tibetan herding, travel and companion dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 209: Tibetan Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard explicitly says it is not a terrier, records herding and trader-watch work, and describes sturdy square medium build, long coat and broad feet.

VBO:0201353.interestingFact: The feet are notably large, flat and round, giving a snowshoe-like spread over rough ground.

VBO:0201374.summary: The Treeing Walker Coonhound is an American raccoon hound bred to follow scent and signal when quarry has climbed a tree. Its long-legged, balanced frame and close tricolor coat suit sustained movement through woods; voice is as central to its job as nose and stamina.

sources.title: AKC Treeing Walker Coonhound standard
sources.evidence: AKC standard specifies raccoon tracking/treeing, endurance, balanced long-legged build, close coat and tricolor preference.

VBO:0201374.interestingFact: 'Treeing' names the moment the dog keeps a raccoon in a tree and announces its location to the hunter.

VBO:0201401.summary: The Weimaraner is a silver-gray German gundog built to work field, forest and water before and after the shot. Its long, clean lines and strong muscles suit that varied job; records connect the early breed to the Weimar court and later to professional hunters in central Germany.
VBO:0201401.historicalRoots: German versatile pointing and retrieving dog.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 99: Weimaraner
sources.evidence: FCI standard gives German origin, Weimar court history, central German hunter breeding, field/forest/water use and silver-gray athletic form.

VBO:0201401.interestingFact: Its pale gray coat gives it one of the most immediately recognizable silhouettes among continental pointers.

VBO:0201415.summary: The West Highland White Terrier is a compact Scottish earthdog in a crisp white double coat. Strong quarters and short legs made sense among moorland rocks; its Poltalloch roots link it with other west Highland terriers, while the white color became its defining visual signature.

sources.title: Royal Kennel Club: West Highland White Terrier
sources.evidence: Royal Kennel Club traces Poltalloch/Argyllshire development from Cairn-related stock and white coat; FCI standard describes compact strong white-coated terrier.

sources.title: FCI standard No. 85: West Highland White Terrier
sources.evidence: Specifies compact strong build, short muscular legs and harsh white coat.

VBO:0201415.interestingFact: Earlier names included Poltalloch Terrier and Roseneath Terrier.

VBO:0201424.summary: The Wire Fox Terrier is a compact British terrier with a short back, longish narrow head and sharply textured coat. Its forward-folding V ears and quick, tiptoe stance give a ready-to-go look; the wire coat is a defining contrast with the separate smooth-coated Fox Terrier.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 169: Wire Fox Terrier
sources.evidence: FCI standard identifies British origin, compact short-backed build, wiry coat, forward-folded V ears and alert active carriage.

VBO:0201424.interestingFact: The coat should be dense and harsh enough to give a crisp outline, with softer hair underneath.

VBO:0201435.summary: The Xiasi Dog comes from Guizhou in southwestern China, where it is known for a compact, quick-moving body. Its usually white, harsh coat, bristly muzzle and upright triangular ears make a distinctive regional silhouette.

sources.title: Guizhou University: Guizhou Xiasi dog
sources.evidence: Guizhou University breed account identifies the local dog as medium, compact and agile, with a mostly white harsh coat, bristly muzzle hair and upright triangular ears.

VBO:0201435.interestingFact: Stiff, needle-like guard hairs can stand up around the face and muzzle.
